title: Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen (2011 TCC 495)
subject: SR&ED Denied for a Multi-Bins Redesign Without Proof of Technological Uncertainty
summary: Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen, sometimes indexed as 2011 TCC 495 but reported as 2011 TCC 261 and affirmed by 2011 FCA 355, denied SR&ED credits to a Calgary plastics thermoformer for its 2005 Multi-Bins redesign. For Canadian manufacturers, the key takeaway is that failing to prove technological uncertainty beyond routine engineering is fatal to a claim.
metaDescription: Discover the key findings in Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen (2011 TCC 495) from the Tax Court of Canada on SR&ED eligibility.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary and Case Background
Procedural History and Citation Clarification

The decision of the Tax Court of Canada in Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. Her Majesty The Queen, officially reported under neutral citation 2011 TCC 261 (Court File No. 2008-3875(IT)G), and unanimously affirmed by the Federal Court of Appeal in Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen, 2011 FCA 355 (Docket A-222-11), stands as one of the most consequential modern Canadian authorities governing Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentives in the commercial manufacturing sector. While the proceeding is occasionally misidentified in secondary administrative indexes under the citation 2011 TCC 495—which actually corresponds to the unrelated Tax Court of Canada decision in Turnnir v. The Queen issued in the same calendar year—the substantive SR&ED adjudication involving Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. is anchored in Justice Steven K. D'Arcy's reasons for judgment delivered on May 11, 2011, following a General Procedure trial in Calgary, Alberta, and Justice Carolyn Layden-Stevenson's appellate reasons for judgment (concurred in by Justices Evans and Mainville), delivered on December 15, 2011, following a hearing in Calgary on December 14, 2011.

The litigation arose from a Notice of Reassessment issued by the Minister of National Revenue (administered by the Canada Revenue Agency, or CRA) disallowing SR&ED qualified expenditures and associated Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) claimed by the Appellant, Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. ("Jentel"), for its fiscal and taxation year ended October 31, 2005. Both the Tax Court of Canada and the Federal Court of Appeal dismissed the taxpayer's appeals with costs awarded to the Crown, cementing a strict jurisprudential boundary between eligible "experimental development" under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) (the "ITA") and ineligible "routine engineering" or standard commercial product development.
The Taxpayer's Claim and Technical Operations

Jentel commenced commercial operations in the autumn of 1993 in Calgary, Alberta, operating as a specialized plastic sheet thermoformer. The corporation developed and manufactured engineered thermoformed plastic components for industrial and consumer markets, dividing its operations between custom contract manufacturing for third-party clients—producing items such as industrial enclosures, commercial displays, and tote bins—and the fabrication of its proprietary product line known as "Multi-Bins". Originally developed in prior fiscal periods, the legacy Multi-Bins product was a small-parts storage system comprising a plastic back panel onto which thermoformed plastic bin fronts were mechanically fastened with screws in rows. Configurable either as a wall-mounted assembly or a standalone floor unit, the system was marketed for organizing small hardware and components across manufacturing workstations, maintenance depots, and residential workshops.

During its 2005 fiscal year, Jentel initiated an extensive engineering overhaul of the Multi-Bins platform. As formally stipulated in paragraphs 8 through 14 of the parties' Statement of Agreed Facts (the "SAF"), the overarching purpose of the 2005 initiative was to improve the existing product to create a smaller, significantly lighter storage system that would require less direct labour to manufacture, offer simpler installation, and consume less energy during transportation. To guide this overhaul, Jentel established five specific, measurable performance objectives: increasing the system's volumetric storage capacity to 20 cubic feet per square metre of floor footprint, representing double the prevailing industry standard; engineering each individual bin front to support a structural load of 100 pounds; developing an integrated "snap-fit" mechanical retention geometry for the bin fronts to eliminate screws and hardware fasteners; introducing full system modularity; and substituting recyclable thermoplastic resins, such as polypropylene, in place of non-recyclable structural engineering plastics such as acrylonitrile butadiene styrene (ABS).

In its SR&ED technical submission (Form T661) to the CRA, Jentel organized its 2005 experimental activities across four distinct component workstreams encompassing bin front and back panels, stands, sliders, and dividers. Within the first workstream focusing on the bin front and back panels, Jentel performed a series of tests under a variety of moulding conditions utilizing at least eight distinct thermoplastic sheet materials: polyethylene terephthalate glycol (PETG), polyvinyl chloride (PVC), acrylic, ABS, styrene, polycarbonate (Lexan), high-density polyethylene (HDPE), and standard polyethylene. For the ABS and HDPE candidates, Jentel conducted subsequent structural strength testing across varying sheet gauges. Additionally, Jentel incorporated a thermal control technique described by its President, Mr. Ralph Hahn, as a "heat sink" or "plug-assist" (freezing) mechanism during the sheet thermoforming cycle.

In the second workstream addressing structural stands, Jentel built test stands using different materials for some of the components: wood, a wood/plastic combination, plastic, and aluminum. The tests were performed to measure the performance of components made from these materials against defined design and manufacturing criteria, and load testing showed that aluminum was the best suited for the application. In the third workstream involving sliders, Jentel designed, fabricated, and tested numerous geometric configurations and profiles for sliding mechanisms; however, none of the prototype sliders operated satisfactorily during the 2005 taxation year. Finally, in the fourth workstream concerning dividers, Jentel performed a series of tests in attempts to determine a method for moulding a groove in the front panel of the Multi-Bins to receive and hold the divider. Across these trials, Jentel tested three separate moulds fabricated from different casting materials and evaluated numerous iterations of groove geometry, in an attempt to create a groove that could be manufactured on a consistent basis, and each of these attempts failed. Crucially, the Crown agreed in the SAF that contemporaneous records were kept for the work in all four technical areas, and that the work on the bin front and back panels and on the stands was performed in a systematic manner (the SAF contains no corresponding "systematic manner" stipulation for the sliders or the dividers).
The Tax Authority's Challenge

The Minister denied Jentel's claim for SR&ED credits on the basis that the work it performed did not meet the definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1) of the ITA, issuing a Notice of Reassessment for the fiscal year ended October 31, 2005. In the Reply to the Notice of Appeal, the Minister of National Revenue anchored the reassessment on two central assumptions of fact: first, that Jentel failed to demonstrate a systematic investigation carried out through experiment or analysis to resolve genuine scientific or technological uncertainties arising during the development of the Multi-Bins system or its constituent parts; and second, that the activities constituted standard commercial product development utilizing routine engineering rather than work undertaken to achieve a scientific or technological advancement.

At trial, the Crown tendered the testimony of Mr. Phillip Leong, a research technology advisor (RTA) for the CRA. In a notable procedural ruling, Justice D'Arcy found both Mr. Hahn and Mr. Leong to be credible individuals, but assigned zero evidentiary weight to Mr. Leong's testimony on the ground that most of his evidence was, in the judge's view, opinion evidence; the reasons for judgment give no further explanation and do not address whether Mr. Leong had been qualified or tendered as an expert witness under the Tax Court of Canada Rules (General Procedure). Consequently, the trial turned entirely on whether the facts agreed to in the SAF, supplemented by the factual testimony of Mr. Hahn, satisfied the statutory threshold under the ITA.
Governing Statutory and Jurisprudential Framework in Canada

In Canadian federal income tax law, the statutory gateway for SR&ED tax incentives is the definition of "scientific research and experimental development" housed in subsection 248(1) of the ITA. Once work satisfies subsection 248(1), current and capital expenditures (prior to the 2014 legislative repeal of capital expenditure eligibility) incurred in Canada are deductible from business income on an indefinite carry-forward basis under subsection 37(1), and "qualified expenditures" as defined in subsection 127(9) and Part XXIX (section 2900) of the Income Tax Regulations, C.R.C., c. 945, generate Investment Tax Credits, including the enhanced 35% refundable ITC for Canadian-controlled private corporations up to their annual expenditure limit or the basic ITC rate, which was 20% for taxation years ending before 2014 (including Jentel's 2005 taxation year) and is 15% for taxation years ending after 2013, prorated for taxation years that include January 1, 2014. Unused ITCs may be carried back three taxation years or carried forward 20 taxation years. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the expenditure limit for the enhanced rate is $6 million, and the enhanced rate is also available to eligible Canadian public corporations.

Subsection 248(1) defines SR&ED as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis" encompassing basic research in paragraph (a), applied research in paragraph (b), and, most commonly in the commercial manufacturing context, experimental development under paragraph (c). Paragraph 248(1)(c) defines experimental development as "work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products or processes, including incremental improvements thereto". Explicit statutory exclusions in paragraphs 248(1)(e) through (k) disqualify routine commercial activities such as market research, quality control, routine testing of materials or products, research in the social sciences, style changes, and commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product.

Because the statutory text does not exhaustively define "technological advancement" or "systematic investigation," Canadian courts evaluate eligibility under the five-question judicial test formulated by Justice Bowman in the landmark decision Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 98 D.T.C. 1839, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520 (TCC), and formally adopted by the Federal Court of Appeal in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, 99 D.T.C. 5087 (FCA) and C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393, 2002 D.T.C. 6740. Under the first criterion, the court asks whether there was a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures. Under the second criterion, the inquiry focuses on whether the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty. The third criterion examines whether the procedure adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses. The fourth criterion asks whether the process resulted in a technological advancement. Finally, the fifth criterion evaluates whether a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and results was kept as the work progressed.

Under the Northwest Hydraulic doctrine, "routine engineering" describes techniques, procedures, and data that are generally accessible to competent professionals in the field. If a technical problem can be resolved with a reasonably predictable outcome using established engineering methodologies—even if achieving that outcome requires extensive effort, iterative adjustments, or substantial expense—there is no technological uncertainty, and the project fails at the threshold.
The Court's Final Holding

Justice D'Arcy dismissed Jentel's appeal, holding that none of the activities performed during the 2005 fiscal year constituted SR&ED under subsection 248(1) of the ITA. The Tax Court concluded that there was no evidence that Jentel's work involved genuine technological risk or uncertainty that could not be resolved through routine engineering. Specifically, thermoforming and injection moulding were well-known, mature manufacturing processes accessible to competent professionals in the plastics industry, and Jentel's testing of different off-the-shelf plastic resins, sheet thicknesses, casting moulds, stand materials, and pre-existing "plug-assist" forming techniques merely represented the use of existing manufacturing processes and existing materials to build an improved commercial product while controlling tooling and manufacturing costs. Furthermore, Justice D'Arcy rejected the Appellant's burden-shifting argument under Hickman Motors Ltd. v. Canada, [1997] 2 S.C.R. 336, holding that because Jentel's own evidence established only routine engineering and standard product development, the Appellant failed to establish a prima facie case capable of demolishing the Minister's assumptions.

On further appeal, the Federal Court of Appeal (2011 FCA 355) unanimously upheld Justice D'Arcy's judgment. Writing for the appellate panel, Justice Layden-Stevenson confirmed that while the identification of the legal test for SR&ED is reviewable on a standard of correctness, the application of the Northwest Hydraulic criteria to the evidence is a question of mixed fact and law subject to appellate intervention only for a "palpable and overriding error" under Housen v. Nikolaisen, 2002 SCC 33. The Federal Court of Appeal ruled that the failure to establish the first criterion—technological uncertainty—is legally dispositive, obviating any need for the trial judge to evaluate the remaining four criteria. Over a decade later, in Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. The Queen, 2021 FCA 88, the Federal Court of Appeal reaffirmed Jentel alongside RIS-Christie and C.W. Agencies as binding appellate authority governing the strict application of the Northwest Hydraulic criteria to manufacturing claims.
2. Core Legal and Evidentiary Failures

A rigorous post-mortem of Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen reveals a striking paradox: the taxpayer secured a formal pre-trial stipulation from the Crown confirming that its bin panel and stand work was performed in a "systematic manner" and that "contemporaneous records" were kept for all four areas of its work, and the trial judge placed no weight on the testimony of the CRA's technical reviewer, yet the taxpayer still suffered a total loss at both the Tax Court and the Federal Court of Appeal. Dissecting the precise legal, technical, contractual, and evidentiary deficiencies that caused this outcome exposes the structural vulnerabilities that routinely undermine Canadian manufacturing SR&ED claims.
Conflation of Commercial Performance Objectives with Technological Uncertainty

The foundational failure in Jentel was the taxpayer's inability to articulate or prove a genuine "technological uncertainty" (Criterion 1 of Northwest Hydraulic), instead presenting ambitious commercial, ergonomic, and functional product design objectives as if they were scientific obstacles. In paragraph 9 of the SAF, Jentel defined its project goals purely in terms of functional output specifications: doubling volumetric storage capacity to 20 cubic feet per square metre, achieving a 100-pound bin front load rating, creating a screwless "snap-fit" assembly, introducing modularity, and transitioning from non-recyclable ABS to recyclable polypropylene.

Under Canadian SR&ED jurisprudence, a product design objective—no matter how aggressive relative to current commercial competitors—is not a technological uncertainty. Technological uncertainty arises only when the underlying scientific or engineering knowledge base of a competent professional is insufficient to predict whether a physical, chemical, metallurgical, or thermodynamic objective can be achieved, or when conflicting technical constraints create a system-level impasse that standard engineering formulas and reference data cannot resolve. In Jentel, the taxpayer never established why standard polymer mechanics or structural engineering design principles could not predict whether a given wall thickness of HDPE, ABS, or polypropylene would support a 100-pound load, or why standard snap-fit cantilever beam equations could not be applied to thermoformed bin fronts. By framing the uncertainty around which off-the-shelf material or geometric profile would perform best, Jentel described an exercise in comparative material selection and empirical design optimization rather than an investigation into an unknown realm of polymer science.
Economic and Tooling Cost Constraints Mistaken for Technological Obstacles

A closely related substantive failure emerged during Mr. Hahn's oral testimony regarding the distinction between thermoforming and injection moulding (paragraphs 18 to 22 of the Tax Court reasons). Mr. Hahn testified that there are hundreds of different types of plastics that could be injection moulded for Jentel's purposes, noting that once an injection mould is designed it cannot be changed and will always produce the same part. Justice D'Arcy observed that the primary constraint with respect to injection moulding appeared to be the cost of the mould, while Mr. Hahn explained that the main difference between the two processes was flexibility, because a thermoformer can manipulate the thermoforming process to achieve a variation in the part; Mr. Hahn also described how Jentel used both thermoforming and injection moulding in attempting to design a better Multi-Bin, and the Federal Court of Appeal noted that Jentel had previously used both methods and did not suddenly begin to use them in its 2005 fiscal year.

Justice D'Arcy relied on this testimony to conclude that Jentel's evidence simply described the use of existing manufacturing processes in an attempt to build a better product, while controlling manufacturing costs, with no evidence of an attempt to achieve a technological advancement. While attempting to achieve injection-moulded geometric tolerances using lower-cost thermoforming can theoretically involve technological uncertainty if the taxpayer attempts to advance the physical limits of thermoforming rheology (such as overcoming localized biaxial draw-ratio thinning beyond established polymer elongation limits), Jentel failed to frame or evidence its work at that scientific level. Instead, the evidence showed that Jentel simply used existing manufacturing processes (thermoforming and injection moulding), with different moulds, plastics and casting materials, in an attempt to build a better product while controlling manufacturing costs. When a taxpayer uses existing manufacturing processes and existing materials in an attempt to improve an existing product while controlling manufacturing costs, as Jentel did with both thermoforming and injection moulding, the Tax Court treats the activity as routine engineering and standard procedures rather than experimental development.
Self-Defeating Admissions Regarding Pre-Existing Industry Technology

During trial, Jentel attempted to anchor its claim for process-level experimental development on its utilization of a "heat sink" during the thermoforming cycle to control localized plastic cooling and solidification. However, under examination, Mr. Hahn candidly acknowledged that what Jentel termed a "heat sink" was actually "plug-assist" forming (or freezing) technology, and explicitly admitted that plug-assist technology had "been out there for quite some time" (paragraph 23 of the TCC decision; affirmed in 2011 FCA 355).

This admission proved fatal to the process advancement argument. Under the Northwest Hydraulic standard, "routine engineering" encompasses all techniques, procedures, and data generally accessible to competent professionals in the field. Even if a specific manufacturing technique—such as plug-assist thermoforming—is new to the taxpayer's shop floor or is being applied for the first time to a specific proprietary product line, adopting a pre-existing industry practice without modifying its underlying mechanical or thermodynamic principles does not cross the threshold into SR&ED. Jentel provided no evidence that its plug-assist implementation required developing novel thermal conductivity models, novel plug surface coatings to eliminate polymer slip-stick friction, or non-standard kinematic actuation profiles.
Supply Chain and Contractual Opacity: Third-Party Extruder Material Variability

An instructive technical and contractual failure occurred in Jentel's attempt to blame upstream material variability for its thermoforming difficulties. At trial (paragraph 19 of the TCC judgment), Mr. Hahn testified that while 12 different plastics could be extruded for Jentel's applications, Jentel purchased its plastic sheets from third-party extruders who melted resin pellets and extruded them into flat sheets. Mr. Hahn asserted that because the third-party extrusion process altered the physical properties of the base resin, the exact specifications of the incoming extruded sheet were unknown to Jentel, creating uncertainty during thermoforming. On appeal to the Federal Court of Appeal, Jentel argued that Justice D'Arcy had made a binding factual finding that extrusion altered resin properties and thereby erred in law by failing to recognize that this created technological uncertainty.

The Federal Court of Appeal flatly rejected this argument, clarifying that Justice D'Arcy was merely summarizing Mr. Hahn's testimony rather than making a judicial finding of technological uncertainty, and noting that, in any event, the trial judge had concluded that he failed to see how the use of different types of plastic resin or materials constituted SR&ED. From a legal and contractual standpoint, this highlights a critical supply chain deficiency: the reasons for judgment record only that a plastic sheet thermoformer such as Jentel specifies the required gauge, size and type of plastic sheet, and they disclose no evidence of contractual material characterization protocols, rheological certifications (such as melt flow index, molecular weight distribution, or residual extruded orientation stress profiles), or collaborative R&D specifications. Although Justice D'Arcy did not invoke any specific statutory exclusion (he simply stated, at paragraph 24, that he failed to see how the use of different types of plastic resin or materials constituted SR&ED), testing incoming commercial materials to determine their unstated physical properties or suitability for production may also be viewed as falling within the statutory exclusion in paragraph 248(1)(f) of the ITA for "quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products or processes". Furthermore, where a taxpayer relies on third-party extruders or toolmakers without structured SR&ED subcontracts governed by subsection 37(1) and subsection 127(9) of the ITA, any technical uncertainty regarding sheet extrusion remains upstream with the supplier, leaving the downstream thermoformer with mere empirical trial-and-error screening.
The Disconnect Between Systematic Trial-and-Error and the Scientific Method

Perhaps the most nuanced legal lesson in Jentel lies in the interplay between the SAF stipulations and the third and fourth criteria of Northwest Hydraulic. In the SAF, the Crown agreed that Jentel tested eight plastic materials for the panels, four materials for the stands, multiple geometries for the sliders, and three casting mould materials for the divider grooves, and further agreed that contemporaneous records were kept for all of this work and that the panel and stand work (but not the slider or divider work) was performed in a "systematic manner". Moreover, all slider designs and all divider groove moulding attempts ended in complete functional failure.

Jentel assumed that proving systematic testing, contemporaneous record-keeping, and repeated technical failure was sufficient to prove SR&ED. Both the Tax Court and the Federal Court of Appeal rejected the claim notwithstanding these stipulations: Justice D'Arcy did not analyze the second, third or fifth criteria, but held that the work involved routine engineering and standard procedures, that there was no evidence of technological risk or uncertainty, and that there was no evidence of an attempt to achieve a technological advancement (paragraphs 10, 16 and 22), and the Federal Court of Appeal confirmed that his finding on the first criterion was dispositive. In common parlance, testing eight materials or three moulds one after another and logging the pass/fail results is "systematic". In Canadian tax law, however, Criterion 2 and Criterion 3 of Northwest Hydraulic require a systematic investigation that accords with the "total discipline of the scientific method," characterized by trained and systematic observation, quantitative measurement, and the formulation, testing, and modification of causal hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing a technological uncertainty.

Jentel's testing was empirical screening ("Wait-and-See" or Edisonian trial-and-error): building stands out of wood, plastic, and aluminum and load testing them, which showed that aluminum was the best suited for the application; or trying three casting moulds and multiple groove geometries until all failed. At no point did the evidence show that Jentel formulated a scientific hypothesis explaining the physical mechanism of failure (such as thermal contraction differentials across the groove radius during cooling) or analyzed how to advance the underlying technology of thermoforming. Similarly, under Criterion 4, while an SR&ED project does not need to succeed commercially to achieve a "technological advancement" (since disproving a scientific hypothesis and generating new technical knowledge about why a boundary condition cannot be crossed qualifies), repeated failure in routine design iteration yields no advancement in the stock of scientific or technological knowledge.
Evidentiary Strategy Failures: The Statement of Agreed Facts Trap and the Hickman Motors Gambit

From a tax litigation perspective, Jentel is widely recognized by Canadian SR&ED practitioners as a cautionary tale regarding the strategic danger of over-relying on a Statement of Agreed Facts (SAF) and misapplying the burden-shifting doctrine of Hickman Motors Ltd. v. Canada, [1997] 2 S.C.R. 336.

Prior to trial, the parties filed an SAF that summarized Jentel's 2005 work in seven brief paragraphs (paragraphs 8 to 14). While an SAF eliminates the need to adduce primary evidence to prove the agreed facts, relying heavily on a high-level, sanitized SAF instead of introducing the underlying contemporaneous engineering notebooks, quantitative test logs, finite element analyses, and failed physical prototypes severely restricts the evidentiary record available to the trial judge. Even though the SAF stated that contemporaneous records were kept, the reasons for judgment do not indicate that those records were relied upon at trial to demonstrate quantitative scientific hypotheses or non-routine engineering analysis; the Court based its conclusion particularly on the SAF and the testimony of Mr. Hahn (paragraph 28).

Compounding this evidentiary vacuum, Jentel relied on a procedural burden-shifting strategy based on Hickman Motors. Appellant's counsel argued that because Mr. Hahn testified credibly about what Jentel did, why it did it, what competitors were doing, and what existed in the public domain, Jentel had established an uncontradicted prima facie case that "demolished" the Minister's assumptions, shifting the legal onus to the Crown to rebut the claim with affirmative evidence. Justice D'Arcy (at paragraphs 25 to 28) rejected this argument without addressing its legal merits, because the Appellant had not established a prima facie case that it was attempting technological advancement, and the Federal Court of Appeal left that finding undisturbed (2011 FCA 355 at para. 4): in Canadian tax litigation, the initial onus rests on the taxpayer to demolish the Minister's assumptions of fact by establishing a prima facie case. Where the taxpayer's own agreed facts and oral testimony, even when accepted as 100% truthful, describe activities that amount in law to routine engineering and standard product development, the Minister's assumptions are confirmed rather than demolished, and the evidentiary burden never shifts to the Crown.
3. Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory and jurisprudential requirement governing SR&ED eligibility in Canada against Jentel Manufacturing Ltd.'s specific evidentiary and technical failures and the governing judicial standard of proof established in Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen (2011 TCC 261; aff'd 2011 FCA 355).

headers: Taxpayer's Specific Failure in Jentel Manufacturing Ltd.
The Court's Standard of Proof & Judicial Holding

cells: Threshold Gateway: Technological Risk or Uncertainty (Criterion 1)
Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), s. 248(1)(c); Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, 98 D.T.C. 1839 (TCC); C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393.

Jentel framed its project around commercial and functional product targets (20 cu. ft./m² capacity, 100-lb load rating, snap-fit assembly, modularity, recyclable resin substitution) and the goal of controlling manufacturing costs rather than identifying any system-level limitation in polymer physics or thermoforming science.

Dispositive Threshold Standard: The taxpayer must adduce objective technical evidence proving that the obstacle could not be resolved by a competent professional using routine engineering or standard procedures. Failure to prove Criterion 1 is fatal to the entire SR&ED claim and relieves the Court of analyzing Criteria 2 through 5.
Exclusion of Routine Engineering & Standard Procedures (Criterion 1 Corollary & Statutory Exclusions)
Income Tax Act, s. 248(1)(e)–(k); Northwest Hydraulic (TCC); Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen, 2011 TCC 261 at paras. 16–24, aff'd 2011 FCA 355.

Jentel utilized pre-existing, mature thermoforming and injection moulding processes. Mr. Hahn admitted that the "heat sink" was simply "plug-assist" forming technology that had "been out there for quite some time". The Court failed to see how the use of different types of plastic resin or materials constituted SR&ED (para. 24).

Objective Industry Benchmark Standard: Routine engineering encompasses all techniques, procedures, and data generally accessible to competent professionals in the field. Adopting existing industry technology (such as plug-assist) or empirically screening commercial materials (8 plastics, 4 stand materials) to control manufacturing costs is ineligible product development.
Formulation of Causal Scientific Hypotheses (Criterion 2)
Northwest Hydraulic (TCC); Soneil International Ltd. v. The Queen, 2011 TCC 391; Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. The Queen, 2021 FCA 88.

Jentel formulated design goals and material selection matrices (testing PETG, PVC, acrylic, ABS, styrene, Lexan, HDPE, polyethylene; testing wood, plastic, and aluminum stands) rather than testable scientific or engineering hypotheses explaining a causal relationship between process variables and material failure modes.

Causal Hypothesis Standard: The taxpayer must prove the formulation of specific scientific or technological hypotheses aimed directly at reducing or eliminating an identified technological uncertainty, rather than merely proposing candidate commercial materials or geometric shapes to see which meets design criteria.
Accordance with the Total Discipline of the Scientific Method (Criterion 3)
Income Tax Act, s. 248(1) ("systematic investigation or search... by means of experiment or analysis"); Northwest Hydraulic (TCC); Kam-Press (2021 FCA 88).

Although the SAF stipulated that Jentel performed tests in a "systematic manner" for the panels and stands (with contemporaneous records also stipulated for the sliders and dividers), the actual methodology consisted of empirical trial-and-error screening without quantitative root-cause analysis or iterative modification of scientific hypotheses.

Scientific Method Discipline Standard: A "systematic" shop-floor workflow or methodical trial-and-error does not satisfy Criterion 3 unless it accords with established and objective principles of the scientific method: trained and systematic observation, quantitative measurement, experiment, and iterative hypothesis modification.
Achievement of Attempted Technological Advancement (Criterion 4)
Income Tax Act, s. 248(1)(c); Northwest Hydraulic (TCC); Jentel Manufacturing (2011 TCC 261 at paras. 22–28; 2011 FCA 355).

Jentel equated product improvements (lighter weight, higher storage density, aluminum stand selection) and repeated component failures (all slider profiles and all 3 divider groove casting moulds failed) with technological advancement, without demonstrating any advancement in underlying thermoforming or polymer knowledge.

Advancement of Technological Knowledge Standard: Incremental product improvements qualify under s. 248(1)(c) only if sought through experimental development aimed at advancing the underlying technology. Neither building a better commercial product via existing processes nor experiencing repeated failure in routine design iteration constitutes a technological advancement.
Contemporaneous Documentation & Evidentiary Burden of Proof (Criterion 5 & Litigation Onus)
Northwest Hydraulic (TCC); Hickman Motors Ltd. v. Canada, [1997] 2 S.C.R. 336; 116736 Canada Inc. v. The Queen (TCC, 1998); Jentel Manufacturing (2011 TCC 261 at paras. 2–3, 25–28).

Despite the SAF stipulating that "contemporaneous records of this work were kept," Jentel relied on a high-level 7-paragraph SAF summary and generalized lay testimony from its President rather than introducing detailed experimental records proving technological uncertainty. Jentel argued that Mr. Hahn's evidence established a prima facie case that demolished the Minister's assumptions and shifted the onus to the Minister under Hickman Motors.

Prima Facie Demolishing Standard: Stipulating that contemporaneous records exist is useless if the substantive content of the evidence shows only routine engineering. To shift the burden to the Minister under Hickman Motors, the taxpayer's evidence (written and oral) must establish a prima facie case of technological uncertainty and attempted advancement.

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the lessons of Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen into actionable legal and technical compliance protocols for Canadian corporate taxpayers, the following two applied industry case studies examine realistic manufacturing projects confronting the exact legal pitfalls identified by Justice D'Arcy and the Federal Court of Appeal. Each case study demonstrates step-by-step how a Canadian taxpayer must restructure its project governance, technical documentation, third-party contract terms, and experimentation tracking to overcome the Jentel objections and satisfy subsection 248(1), section 37, and subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act.
Case Study 1: Advanced Thermoforming & Polymer Processing (Recycled Polypropylene Thin-Wall Structural Snap-Fit Enclosures)
Scenario and Exposure to the Jentel Pitfalls

AltaForm Plastics Inc. ("AltaForm"), a Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) operating a heavy-gauge sheet thermoforming facility in Calgary, Alberta, manufactures proprietary modular industrial battery enclosures. To meet new industrial sustainability mandates and double volumetric stacking density, AltaForm initiates a project to replace its legacy 6.0 mm virgin ABS enclosure panels (assembled with steel bolts) with a 3.2 mm 100% post-consumer recycled polypropylene (rPP) panel featuring an integrated, high-retention thermoformed snap-fit undercut groove capable of withstanding 120 lbs of dynamic shear load without fasteners.

Initially, AltaForm operates exactly as Jentel did: its shop floor supervisor orders extruded sheets of eight different commercial rPP, HDPE, and PETG blends from a third-party extruder, installs a standard mechanical plug-assist ("heat sink") on the thermoforming press, fabricates three cast-aluminum moulds with varying undercut groove radii, and runs 40 shop-floor trials. Every rPP snap-fit groove either tears during demoulding or suffers brittle stress-whitening failure under a 70-lb load. If audited or litigated in this state, AltaForm's SR&ED claim will be summarily disallowed under Jentel (2011 TCC 261; 2011 FCA 355) on the grounds that thermoforming, plug-assist tooling, and testing commercial resin sheets to reduce weight and eliminate fasteners constitute routine engineering and standard product development.
Step 1: Restructuring Project Governance and Baseline Benchmarking

To survive judicial scrutiny under Criterion 1 of Northwest Hydraulic and avoid the Jentel trap, AltaForm must immediately separate its commercial product development governance from its SR&ED governance prior to commencing shop-floor trials. AltaForm establishes a formal SR&ED Technical Charter overseen by a qualified Polymer Processing Engineer, who serves as the "competent professional" benchmark required under Northwest Hydraulic.

Before touching the thermoforming press, the governance committee conducts and documents a formal Baseline Literature and Industry Benchmark Review. First, the team excludes the preliminary screening of off-the-shelf commercial plastics (PETG, PVC, ABS, virgin HDPE) from the SR&ED project scope, charging those routine material selection activities to a standard commercial cost centre in accordance with paragraph 248(1)(f) of the ITA. Second, the engineer calculates theoretical wall-thinning and snap-fit cantilever strain using standard thermoforming Finite Element Analysis (FEA) software (such as Ansys Polyflow) and published polymer data sheets. The baseline analysis proves that standard thermoforming of semi-crystalline rPP across a sharp undercut groove (draw ratio exceeding 2.8:1) fails because rPP exhibits an ultra-narrow thermoforming melt window (6°C before sag) and severe bimodal molecular weight degradation from post-consumer recycling, which induces strain-induced crystallization and micro-void tearing during biaxial plug-assist stretching—a phenomenon that standard plug-assist temperature and velocity curves cannot resolve. By establishing that standard plug-assist thermoforming and standard polymer mechanics predict failure, AltaForm isolates a genuine technological uncertainty rather than a commercial design goal.
Step 2: Restructuring Technical Documentation and Hypothesis Formulation

To cure the Jentel failure where functional objectives (100-lb load, modularity, snap-fit) were conflated with scientific hypotheses, AltaForm bans commercial marketing language from its technical records and mandates a structured Technological Uncertainty and Causal Hypothesis Dossier.

Instead of documenting an objective to make a lighter recyclable snap-fit panel supporting 120 lbs, AltaForm documents the exact system-level technological uncertainty: whether a semi-crystalline post-consumer rPP sheet with a heterogeneous melt flow index (2–12 g/10 min) can be biaxially stretched into a negative-draft undercut snap-fit geometry (local draw ratio 3.1:1) without exceeding critical amorphous tie-chain fracture thresholds or suffering post-moulding warpage from anisotropic crystalline shrinkage, given that conventional isothermal plug-assist tooling induces premature surface skin freezing that locks in internal residual shear stresses.

AltaForm then formulates explicit, quantitative causal scientific hypotheses under Criterion 2 prior to each experimental phase. The first primary hypothesis addresses rheological and thermal gradient control, positing that modulating the thermal conductivity gradient across the plug-assist geometry via a zoned, syntactic-foam and beryllium-copper composite plug coupled with pulsed infrared pre-heating will delay surface lamellar crystallization in the rPP sheet by 3.5 seconds during deep-draw extension, thereby maintaining amorphous chain mobility across the undercut radius and preventing micro-void stress whitening. The second primary hypothesis addresses viscoelastic strain recovery during demoulding, positing that introducing a two-stage pneumatic pressure-reversal cycle synchronized with the glass-transition cooling curve of the rPP blend will induce controlled elastic snap-back across the negative-draft groove without exceeding the yield strain (8%) of the thinned wall section during mould stripping.
Step 3: Restructuring Contract Terms and Supply Chain Allocation

In Jentel, Mr. Hahn complained that third-party extruders altered the resin properties during sheet extrusion so that Jentel did not know the exact specifications of the incoming sheets, yet the Court found no evidence that any of Jentel's work involved technological risk or uncertainty and failed to see how the use of different types of plastic resin or materials constituted SR&ED. Similarly, Jentel tried three different moulds made of different casting materials, and the reasons for judgment disclose no evidence that experimental tooling variables were isolated.

AltaForm overhauls its commercial procurement contracts with its Canadian sheet extruder and Canadian mould-maker into formal SR&ED Collaborative Supply and Subcontractor Agreements structured under subsection 37(1) and subsection 127(9) of the ITA. Rather than buying generic commercial sheets under standard purchase orders, AltaForm amends its supply contract with its Canadian extruder to mandate batch-specific Certificate of Analysis (CoA) rheological data for every extruded sheet lot—specifically Differential Scanning Calorimetry (DSC) crystallinity curves, Melt Flow Index (MFI), intrinsic viscosity, and inline extrusion calender orientation ratios. This contractual mandate eliminates unknown commercial specification noise and establishes a known scientific baseline for every sheet entering the experiment. Furthermore, where the Canadian extruder performs custom experimental compounding and co-extrusion trials on AltaForm's behalf, the contract includes an explicit SR&ED Subcontractor Statement of Work (SOW) stipulating that the work is performed in Canada on AltaForm's behalf, vesting 100% of the foreground intellectual property and technical data logs in AltaForm, and pricing the experimental runs on a time-and-materials basis without government or non-government assistance, thereby preventing "contract payment" reductions under subsection 127(9) of the ITA.

Simultaneously, for the three prototype moulds and composite plug-assists, AltaForm structures its contract with the custom machine shop to explicitly segregate routine mould base machining from experimental cavity insert fabrication. Because Canadian tax provisions applicable after 2013 exclude capital expenditures from SR&ED deductions and ITCs, custom moulds must qualify as current expenditures on materials transformed or rendered worthless during experimental trials under paragraph 2900(2)(a) of the Income Tax Regulations and the CRA's SR&ED while Developing an Asset Policy and SR&ED During Production Runs Policy (both dated July 19, 2016). The contract explicitly documents that the three cast and machined prototype inserts are non-durable, single-purpose experimental test fixtures designed to be destructively modified and scrapped during hypothesis testing, rather than depreciable commercial production tooling.
Step 4: Restructuring Experimentation Tracking and Evidentiary Trial Readiness

To overcome the Jentel failure where systematic pass/fail logging and failed divider moulds were held to involve routine engineering and standard procedures, AltaForm replaces generic shop-floor run sheets with a rigorous Design of Experiments (DoE) Parametric Matrix and Failure Mode Analysis Protocol satisfying Criteria 3, 4, and 5.

For every trial run, engineers record independent controlled variables—including sheet core versus surface temperature via thermal imaging, plug-assist velocity profile in mm/s, plug zone temperatures, vacuum draw pressure rise rate in kPa/s, and cooling dwell time—alongside quantitative dependent response metrics, specifically ultrasonic wall-thickness distribution across 18 coordinate points on the snap-fit groove, optical microscopy measurements of crystalline spherulite size and micro-void density, and Instron tensile and shear load-to-failure curves in Newtons. When Mould Iteration 1 and Mould Iteration 2 fail, the engineering team does not simply try a third mould; they perform cross-sectional microscopy and DSC thermal analysis on the failed parts, proving why the initial thermal-gradient hypothesis failed (for instance, demonstrating that rapid conductive heat loss at the plug tip caused a 30% drop in local amorphous tie-chain density), and mathematically reformulate the hypothesis for the subsequent iteration.

Finally, if the claim proceeds to the Tax Court of Canada, tax litigation counsel avoids the Jentel Statement of Agreed Facts trap. Counsel refuses to compress the technical case into a generic seven-paragraph SAF that describes only commercial goals; instead, any partial SAF is restricted to corporate status, fiscal dates, and accounting quantum, while the substantive scientific case is proven at trial by introducing the contemporaneous DoE matrices, FEA models, DSC lab reports, and the oral testimony of the lead Polymer Engineer—supplemented, if necessary, by an independent expert witness properly qualified under Rule 145 of the Tax Court of Canada Rules (General Procedure).
Case Study 2: Precision Metal Stamping & Structural Assembly Manufacturing (High-Strength Lightweight Modular Rack & Slider Systems)
Scenario and Exposure to the Jentel Pitfalls

NorSteel Fabricators Ltd. ("NorSteel"), an Ontario-based CCPC specializing in precision roll-forming, metal stamping, and industrial storage systems, undertakes a project to develop a next-generation high-density modular storage rack and linear drawer-slider system for automated warehouse robotics. The commercial goals mirror Jentel's: reducing system weight by 45%, doubling footprint storage density, supporting a 250-lb dynamic cantilevered load on the linear sliders without ball bearings, and eliminating welded fasteners through a snap-interlock structural column.

Initially, NorSteel's shop-floor team builds prototype stands out of carbon steel, aluminum alloys, and fiberglass composites, load-testing them until aluminum 6061-T6 is selected. Simultaneously, tool-and-die makers design and stamp 14 different geometric profiles of self-lubricating linear sliders and try three progressive stamping die configurations to form an interlocking retention groove in Ultra-High-Strength Steel (UHSS); all slider profiles bind under load and all three stamping dies fail to form the groove consistently due to metal springback. Under Jentel (2011 TCC 261; 2011 FCA 355) and its direct progeny Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. The Queen (2021 FCA 88), the CRA will disallow the entire claim: comparative load-testing of carbon steel, aluminum, and composites is routine material selection, and iterating slider shapes and stamping die grooves on the shop floor without adhering to the scientific method is routine tool-and-die engineering.
Step 1: Restructuring Project Governance and Baseline Benchmarking

NorSteel restructures its project governance by instituting a mandatory SR&ED Eligibility Gate-Review Protocol prior to incurring claimable shop-floor labour or material costs. During the Gate-Review, NorSteel's Chief Metallurgical and Mechanical Engineer bifurcates the project into ineligible commercial engineering and eligible experimental development.

First, the comparative fabrication and load testing of the support stands across carbon steel, aluminum, and composites—where standard structural mechanics, such as Euler buckling and von Mises stress equations, can readily predict deflection and load capacity—is excised from the SR&ED claim and classified as routine commercial design engineering, avoiding the exact error committed in Jentel's "Stands" sub-project (SAF paragraph 12).

Second, the engineering team conducts a documented State-of-the-Art Benchmark Analysis on the failing UHSS interlocking groove and bearingless slider components. The baseline analysis demonstrates that forming a tight-radius (1.5 mm inside radius) re-entrant interlocking groove and bearingless slider track in Dual-Phase 980 MPa Ultra-High-Strength Steel (DP980) cannot be resolved by standard roll-forming or progressive die design rules, such as standard sheet metal bend allowances or standard over-bending compensation tables. Specifically, cold-working the martensitic-ferritic microstructure of DP980 in a compound reverse-bend geometry induces non-linear, asymmetric kinematic hardening (the Bauschinger effect) coupled with severe adiabatic shear band localization, resulting in unpredictable 3D torsional springback (3.5° twist) that causes the bearingless slider rails to gall and seize under cantilevered loads. Because published metallurgical forming limit diagrams (FLDs) do not model coupled biaxial reverse-bend springback in thin-gauge DP980, a genuine technological uncertainty is established.
Step 2: Restructuring Technical Documentation and Hypothesis Formulation

To eliminate the Jentel defect where designing and testing "many various shapes and forms of sliders" and "many iterations of groove design" formed part of the work that the Court held to involve routine engineering and standard procedures (SAF paragraphs 13 and 14), NorSteel replaces shape-iteration logs with a formal Metallurgical and Tribological Hypothesis Framework.

NorSteel documents its technological advancement objective under Criterion 4 not as building a working slider and groove, but as generating new quantitative engineering knowledge characterizing the interaction between multi-axial strain-path reversals, martensitic phase transformation stresses, and micro-textured tribological contact geometry in DP980 UHSS sheet forming.

NorSteel then establishes testable scientific hypotheses under Criterion 2 governing both the stamping die kinematics and the slider tribology. With respect to strain-path reversal and springback compensation, NorSteel hypothesizes that applying a localized, compressive coining pre-strain (8% thickness reduction) along the neutral axis of the DP980 sheet immediately prior to the reverse-bend forming station will disrupt the directional dislocation pile-ups responsible for the Bauschinger effect, equalizing residual through-thickness tangential stresses and reducing longitudinal torsional springback below the 0.5° threshold required for linear slider clearance. Concurrently, with respect to tribological contact mechanics for the bearingless sliders, NorSteel moves away from randomly varying macroscopic slider shapes and hypothesizes that impressing a deterministic sinusoidal micro-dimple array (15 µm depth, 20% area density) into the slider rail contact surface during the final stamping stroke will reduce adhesive Hertzian contact stress peaks and trap solid-film molybdenum disulfide (MoS₂) lubricant platelets, thereby preventing galling and cold-welding under a 250-lb cantilevered moment.
Step 3: Restructuring Contract Terms and Supply Chain Allocation

In commercial metal manufacturing, companies frequently build prototype tooling for customer-funded contracts or rely on external tool-and-die shops and commercial testing laboratories without proper contractual structuring. NorSteel implements strict legal and contractual safeguards across its upstream and downstream agreements to protect its SR&ED tax base.

To achieve customer contract insulation and prevent funded research or contract payment exclusions where a major warehouse automation client expresses interest in purchasing the modular rack system, NorSteel ensures that its commercial supply agreement is strictly a standard contract for the future sale of commercial goods ("off-the-shelf" product pricing) rather than a contract to perform R&D or custom engineering design. Under subsection 127(9) of the ITA, if a Canadian customer pays a taxpayer "to perform SR&ED on behalf of" the customer or reimburses development tooling costs, the payment constitutes a "contract payment" or "assistance" that strips away NorSteel's qualified expenditures dollar-for-dollar. NorSteel drafts its customer contracts to explicitly state that all design, engineering, and experimental development of the proprietary rack and slider technology is undertaken solely at NorSteel's financial risk, that NorSteel retains exclusive legal and beneficial ownership of all resulting intellectual property and tooling, and that customer payments are strictly contingent upon delivery of finished commercial units meeting acceptance specifications.

Furthermore, when engaging a Canadian university metallurgy lab for X-ray diffraction residual stress testing and a Canadian tool-and-die subcontractor to EDM-machine experimental coining inserts, NorSteel executes formal SR&ED Subcontractor Agreements. These contracts specify the exact scientific parameters being tested, mandate the delivery of raw quantitative test data rather than pass/fail certificates, confirm that all work is executed physically within Canada, and separate eligible experimental die inserts—which are consumed and scrapped during iterative coining trials—from non-eligible capital die shoes and press machinery.
Step 4: Restructuring Experimentation Tracking and Evidentiary Trial Readiness

To satisfy Criterion 3 (the scientific method) and Criterion 5 (detailed contemporaneous records), which the courts in Jentel did not need to reach because Criterion 1 was dispositive but which Kam-Press confirmed must be applied, NorSteel institutes a Quantitative Shop-Floor Experimentation and Metrology Protocol.

Rather than recording simple failure notes for slider shapes or groove moulds, every experimental stamping trial is linked to a specific mathematical prediction in the Yoshida-Uemori kinematic hardening model. Following each press stroke, NorSteel measures the formed DP980 rail using a 3D laser Coordinate Measuring Machine (CMM) to generate a continuous deviation heat-map of springback angles (Δθ) and torsional twist (φ) relative to the theoretical hypothesis. Slider prototypes are evaluated on an instrumented tribometer that continuously logs coefficient of friction (μ), acoustic emission spikes indicating incipient galling, and wear-track depth profilometry across 10,000 reciprocation cycles.

Crucially, even if all three experimental die iterations fail to achieve commercial manufacturability by year-end—just as Jentel's sliders and divider grooves failed—NorSteel's contemporaneous documentation proves that each failure was analyzed via X-ray diffraction and CMM metrology to falsify a specific scientific hypothesis and quantify the exact boundary conditions where coining pre-strain triggers brittle martensitic micro-cracking in DP980. This documented acquisition of new metallurgical and tribological knowledge satisfies Criterion 4 (technological advancement) regardless of commercial product failure, rendering the claim resilient against both CRA technical audit and Tax Court litigation.
Summary Matrix of Remedial Restructuring Across Both Case Studies
The table below synthesizes the structural transformation from the non-compliant Jentel posture to the fully compliant SR&ED legal and technical posture demonstrated in Case Studies 1 and 2.

body.text: 5. Conclusions and Strategic Takeaways for Canadian SR&ED Practitioners

The jurisprudence established by the Tax Court of Canada and the Federal Court of Appeal in Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen (2011 TCC 261; aff'd 2011 FCA 355) remains a definitive legal touchstone for evaluating manufacturing and shop-floor SR&ED claims in Canada. The rulings demonstrate that the five criteria of Northwest Hydraulic operate as a cumulative, hierarchical legal filter in which the first criterion—the existence of a technological risk or uncertainty that cannot be resolved through routine engineering or standard procedures—is strictly dispositive. Where a taxpayer's activities consist of utilizing mature manufacturing processes, adopting pre-existing industry techniques such as plug-assist thermoforming, or empirically screening commercial materials and geometric configurations to achieve functional product improvements while controlling manufacturing costs, no amount of methodical shop-floor record-keeping or repeated component failure will elevate the work into eligible experimental development under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act.

Furthermore, Jentel underscores a vital procedural lesson for tax litigation counsel appearing before the Tax Court of Canada. Relying on a condensed Statement of Agreed Facts and attempting to shift the evidentiary burden onto the Crown under Hickman Motors will fail if the taxpayer's affirmative evidence does not first establish a prima facie case of genuine technological uncertainty and scientific investigation. By proactively segregating routine commercial engineering from experimental development at the governance level, benchmarking the exact limits of standard engineering knowledge, formulating causal scientific hypotheses, structuring supply chain and customer contracts to preserve qualified expenditures, and maintaining quantitative parametric test records, Canadian manufacturers can successfully navigate the strict evidentiary standards enforced by the courts.
